notes:
I've grouped the notes by verse. Some verses share one entry when the commentators discuss them together. At the end I list what I couldn't find.

**vv. 1–2: "I have hardened his heart… that you may tell your children"**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says God hardened Pharaoh's heart here, but Exodus 9:34 says Pharaoh hardened his own. Both were true, and one does not deny the other. In his reading, God let Pharaoh have the hard heart he sinfully wanted. The plagues were also meant to encourage later generations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Ellicott says Pharaoh's officials had first hardened their own hearts (9:34), so they deserved a penal hardening. He also says there is nothing unworthy of God in using such a hardening for His glory and for the good of future generations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10.htm
- Gill notes that some translate "for I have hardened" as "though I have hardened." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10.htm
- **NET notes:** the theme is repeated so often that it must not be minimized: God was laying the foundation of Israel's faith in His sovereignty. The verb in v. 2 is a bold word meaning to toy with or "make fools" of the Egyptians. Some translate it "dealt ruthlessly" instead. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10
- Precept Austin says the hardening led to three more signs: locusts, darkness and the death of the firstborn. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-10-commentary

**Where traditions differ: the hardening (vv. 1, 20, 27)**
- **Reformed/Baptist (Piper):** Piper concedes that God never hardens anyone who had not first hardened himself, which makes the hardening a judicial act, abandoning him to his own stubbornness. But he reads Romans 9 as teaching that hardening is ultimately unconditional, coming from the free and wise and sovereign will of the potter. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-hardening-of-pharaoh-and-the-hope-of-the-world
- **A different view (Gospel Coalition Canada column):** Of the 20 references to the hardening, 10 hold Pharaoh responsible. God isn't said to act on Pharaoh's heart until chapter 9. The column quotes a scholar who sees the hardening as a temporary act for a specific purpose, not eternal rejection. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/did-god-harden-pharaohs-heart/
- **Lutheran (Luther, as reported by Ligonier):** Luther held that God puts no new evil in the heart. All that God must do to harden anyone's heart is to withhold His own grace. https://www.ligonier.org/posts/understanding-free-will
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God used natural means as far as possible, even while punishing Egypt by miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html
- **Catholic:** A Catholic Answers reply says the "God hardened" wording stresses that no other god was at work. In modern terms we would say God *permitted* Pharaoh's hardening. https://www.catholic.com/qa/did-god-negate-pharaohs-free-will. Joe Heschmeyer quotes Spurgeon: the same sun that melts wax hardens clay. He argues Pharaoh hardens himself in response to what God does. https://www.catholic.com/video/why-did-god-harden-pharaohs-heart-in-exodus
- **Church Fathers:** Origen asked why Pharaoh's heart needed hardening several times unless indeed because it was possible for him to yield to persuasion. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04123.htm

**v. 3: "How long will you refuse to humble yourself?"**
- Guzik: pride was Pharaoh's real problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Pulpit: Pharaoh's earlier confession (9:27) was cancelled by his later defiance, and God wanted submission in action, not humble words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html
- NET: the question is partly rhetorical, since God was not yet finished humbling Pharaoh. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10
- Matthew Henry: Those that will not humble themselves God will humble. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_010.cfm

**vv. 4–6: The locusts announced**
- Precept Austin: naming "tomorrow" showed the swarm came from God and was not a random natural event. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-10-commentary
- Pulpit: the delay gave the king time to repent. Eastern houses had only lattice windows, so locusts could get inside. Locust invasions were rare in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html
- NET: the Hebrew word for locust comes from a root meaning "to be many." People dreaded locusts and had gods to call on against them. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10

**v. 7: The officials' plea**
- Guzik: even the officials gave in, but Pharaoh's heart was harder still. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- NET: "snare" is a bird trap. By blaming "this man," the officials avoid naming Yahweh or blaming Pharaoh. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10

**vv. 8–11: "Who exactly will be going?" / "Only the men"**
- Guzik: Pharaoh wanted to keep the women and children as hostages. Many people want to "give in" to God without fully submitting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- NET on v. 10: Pharaoh's words are no blessing. Cassuto paraphrases them as: may God's help be as far from you as I am from letting you go. The irony is that Pharaoh did let them go and the Lord was with them. "Little ones" means all dependents. The word for "men" in v. 11 means strong men. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10
- Pulpit: Pharaoh must have known women and children attended his own festivals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html
- **Methodist (Wesley) on v. 10:** Satan tries to stop believers from bringing their children to God. He is a sworn enemy to early piety. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) calls it an insidious compromise. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/exodus-10.html

**vv. 12–15: The locusts arrive**
- Guzik: Yahweh showed Himself greater than Osiris, thought to protect the crops. God exposes the false gods we trust. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Pulpit: locust columns of 500 miles have been recorded, and widths of 20 miles, but never both together, so this swarm was plainly abnormal. The "darkened" land could mean the swarm in flight or settled on the ground. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html

**vv. 16–20: Pharaoh's confession and the west wind**
- Guzik: this was a false repentance, words without action. He quotes Cole on the easy confession of sin that only wants to avoid the consequences. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- NET: Since his heart was not yet submissive, his confession was vain. http://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Exo&chapter=10
- Matthew Henry: Pharaoh wanted rid of the locusts, not of the more dangerous plague of a hard heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_010.cfm
- Pulpit: to carry the locusts into the Red Sea (literally "Sea of Weeds"), the wind must have blown from the northwest. In v. 20 the verb for hardening is a stronger word than the one used earlier. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-20.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: the removal of the locusts showed the hardened king how patient God was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-20.htm

**vv. 21–23: Darkness that can be felt**
- Guzik: like the third and sixth plagues, this one came without warning. It was supernatural and struck at the sun god Ra. Lamps may not have worked. Scripture doesn't say whether Israel's light was natural or supernatural. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Calvin: no warning came because Pharaoh had broken his promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/10-21.html
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the Hebrew means "one shall grasp darkness," which is hyperbole. To Egyptians it would look as if Ra had died. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-21.htm
- **Natural-cause readings:** Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes, Constable and Coffman link it to the khamsin dust storm, made worse by God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-21.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/10-21.html. Against this, the NET calls Driver's sandstorm theory "antisupernatural." Pharaoh would not have been frightened by an ordinary seasonal wind. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=exo+10%3A21-23. Biblehub's study notes also say it was no eclipse or sandstorm. https://biblehub.com/exodus/10-21.htm
- Matthew Henry records a Jewish tradition that evil spirits terrified Egypt during the darkness (compare Psalm 78:49). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-21.htm

**vv. 24–26: "Not a hoof will be left behind"**
- Guzik: God refuses every attempt to give Him less than everything. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Pulpit: forbidding the flocks made no sense when the whole point was to sacrifice. Pharaoh still couldn't grasp that Jehovah is not to be bargained with. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-10.html
- NET (quoted by Precept Austin): Moses would leave Pharaoh no pledge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-10-commentary

**vv. 28–29: "You will never see my face again"**
- Guzik: Moses' agreement was bad news for Pharaoh. He quotes Morgan: "Pharaoh was now beyond reason, and God did not reason with him." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-10/
- Matthew Henry: when people drive God's word away, He leaves them to their own delusions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/10-21.htm

**What I couldn't find:** I found nothing from a Pentecostal, Anglican or Orthodox source. Guzik's site is on your Pentecostal list, but he writes from Calvary Chapel, not as a Pentecostal. I also found no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. For a Lutheran view I only have Ligonier's report of Luther, nothing from lcms.org or 1517.org. I didn't find a Bible Odyssey article on Exodus 10. The NET notes I read stopped at v. 11, so there is nothing from them on vv. 12–29 beyond the darkness page.
